newsitem.title: USA: U.S. strains to find jobs for welfare recipients.
newsitem.headline: U.S. strains to find jobs for welfare recipients.

text.p: Straining to find a million jobs for people who will lose aid under a new welfare law, President Clinton has turned to a solution his administration fought in the past -- tax breaks for business.
In 1994 the White House asked Congress to kill a federal tax credit for firms that hired disadvantaged workers, saying it gave companies a financial windfall but did little to generate employment.

Now Clinton has become a tax-credit booster, asking Congress to create a bigger, more generous break for companies hiring welfare recipients. It is part of his overall plan to move one million welfare recipients into jobs by 2000.

Congressional Republicans agreed to make welfare-to-work a top priority during a meeting with Clinton last month. They are leery, but, like the president, eager to show they are serious about making the welfare law perform.

"We are in the same position as Clinton in saying we want to do something to stimulate jobs in cities. This looks like it does something even though it doesn't," said a Republican aide. "Substantively it's bad, politically it's good."

Republicans cite a history of studies showing the targeted jobs tax credit, which the White House wanted to repeal, and other wage subsidies were not effective in moving people to jobs. In fact, they sometimes were a disincentive to hiring.
A Labour Department audit of the targeted jobs credit found 92 percent of workers would have been hired without it.

Employers were checking records only after hiring workers to see if they were eligible for the credit. Most hires were in low-skill, high-turnover jobs. Overall, the credit returned less than 40 cents in benefits for every dollar spent.
Congress let the credit die in 1994, but created a successor tax break last year as part of a minimum wage law.
Acting Labour Secretary Cynthia Metzler said the problems that plagued the former credit were addressed in last year's "work opportunity tax credit" and Clinton's welfare plan.
Those fixes, however, do not mesh with the interests of business, whose support will be vital to Clinton's efforts.
"These tax incentives are just one piece of an overall strategy," Metzler said. "We have confidence ... this programme is more likely to work."

While studies found wage subsidies may act as red flags to certain employers, discouraging them from taking on what appear to be hard-to-hire individuals, Metzler said, Clinton's strong effort to sell the welfare initiative could mitigate such concerns.
"There is a positive outcry and outpouring of attention right now about moving people from welfare to work. I don't think the stigma is as great," she said.

The overall White House plan, estimated to cost $552 million over five years, would let businesses deduct half of the first $10,000 in wages to longer-term welfare recipients. Companies could count training, child care, transportation and other expenses as wages.
It also extends the work opportunity tax credit, which allows employers to deduct 35 percent of first $6,000 in wages for shorter-term welfare recipients, former felons and others.

The tax breaks are part of a White House effort to cajole businesses into hiring welfare recipients under the law, which limits benefits to five years. Clinton wants billions of dollars for jobs and is relying on moral suasion, telling corporate leaders it is their civic duty to make the law work.

"It certainly is a larger sum of money to dangle in front of the eyes of employers," said Gary Burtless, a Brookings Institution expert. "The president has spent a lot more time trying to get the business community involved and interested in the (tax) credit than any president up to now."

Big business has long been the biggest fan of such tax breaks. But business lobbyists are already trying to figure out how to "fix" the Clinton plan. They want to water down some safeguards, like the requirement that new hires work more hours.
"Increasing the hours ... makes it not user friendly," said Kathleen O'Leary of the National Restaurant Association.
Others don't want two credits and, instead of targeting welfare recipients, want to expand the pool of eligible hires.
"If people don't have basic skills and aren't trainable, ... people are going to be reluctant to give them a job for a $5,000 credit," said Bill Signer, who represents large firms.
